decisions.title: What risk tier is this AI system?
decisions.short: Work out whether a system is prohibited, high-risk, limited-risk, or minimal-risk under the EU AI Act — and record why.
decisions.why: Classification determines which obligations apply and by when. It is the decision every other AI Act obligation depends on, and the one most often left undone because the definitions are hard to apply to a real system.
decisions.intro: Answer about ONE system at a time. Take the system as it actually operates, not as it was described in the business case. If two answers seem true, pick the stronger one — over-classifying costs effort, under-classifying costs a great deal more.

questions.text: Does the system infer people's emotions in a workplace or an educational setting?
questions.help: Includes tone or sentiment analysis of employee messages, engagement or attention monitoring, and mood detection in interviews. Detecting emotion for medical or safety reasons is treated differently — if that is your case, answer No and note it.

questions.text: Does it score or rank people's trustworthiness or social behaviour, in a way that could disadvantage them in an unrelated context?
questions.help: The test is unrelated context: using payment history to decide credit is ordinary; using it to restrict access to a school place is not.

questions.text: Does it use subliminal or deliberately manipulative techniques, or exploit someone's age, disability, or economic vulnerability, in a way likely to cause harm?
questions.help: Ordinary persuasion and marketing are not caught. What is caught is technique designed to bypass conscious decision-making, or targeting that works precisely because the person is vulnerable.

questions.text: Does it do real-time remote biometric identification in a public space, scrape facial images untargeted from the internet or CCTV, or infer protected characteristics from biometrics?
questions.help: Protected characteristics here means race, political opinion, trade union membership, religion, sex life, or sexual orientation. Verifying one person against their own stored image — unlocking a phone — is not this.

questions.text: Does it predict whether an individual will commit a crime, based only on profiling or personality traits?
questions.help: Assessing a specific, already-suspected individual on objective facts is different from profiling the general population.

questions.text: Is the system used in any of these areas?
questions.help: Pick the closest match. These are the Annex III areas where AI is treated as high-risk because of what is at stake for the person affected.

options.label: Employment — recruitment, screening, promotion, task allocation, or monitoring
Essential services — credit scoring, insurance pricing, or access to public benefits
Healthcare triage, or emergency service dispatch
Law enforcement, migration, border control, or justice
Biometric identification or categorisation (where not prohibited above)
Critical infrastructure — safety in water, gas, electricity, or transport

questions.text: Is the system a safety component of a product that already needs third-party conformity assessment?
questions.help: Think medical devices, machinery, lifts, vehicles, toys. If your product already carries a CE mark under its own regulation and this AI affects its safety, that is Annex I.

questions.text: Does the system only perform a narrow procedural task, improve the result of prior human work, detect patterns without replacing human assessment, or do preparatory work?
questions.help: This is the Art. 6(3) narrowing, and it is the most commonly over-claimed provision in the Act. Be honest: if the human who reviews the output almost always accepts it, the system is not merely preparatory — it is deciding.
questions.unsure_note: Not sure means the derogation does not apply. The burden of showing it does is on you, so treat the system as fully high-risk until you can evidence otherwise.

questions.text: Does the system profile people — that is, does it evaluate or predict anything about an individual's characteristics, behaviour, performance, or circumstances?
questions.help: Ranking, scoring, or predicting anything about a person counts, even if a human signs off afterwards. Screening job applicants, scoring credit applicants, or predicting who will leave are all profiling. Detecting duplicate records or extracting a date from a form is not.
questions.unsure_note: Not sure means treat it as profiling. The derogation is unavailable to profiling systems with no exceptions, so this is the safer reading.

questions.text: Do people interact with this system directly — a chatbot, a voice agent, an assistant?
questions.help: The question is whether a person could be talking to it, not whether they usually realise they are.

questions.text: Does it generate or materially alter image, audio, video, or text published to the public?
questions.help: Includes marketing copy, synthetic voice, and edited imagery. Internal drafting that a human rewrites before publication is not this.

questions.text: Does it do emotion recognition or biometric categorisation in a setting that is permitted?
questions.help: You will have answered No to the workplace and education question earlier. If you use neither at all, answer No.

outcomes.headline: Stop. This looks like a prohibited practice.
outcomes.detail: Practices banned under Article 5 have been unlawful since 2 February 2025, and carry the highest penalty tier. There is no transition period left and no compliance route — the system cannot be brought into compliance by adding controls.
actions: Do not deploy it. If it is live, suspend it now and notify your committee within 24 hours.
Record the decision, the date, and who made it.
Get legal advice before restarting any related work.
Check whether anything else in your estate does the same thing.
outcomes.counsel: The Article 5 prohibitions have carve-outs and definitional edges that matter enormously here. Confirm with qualified counsel before you either proceed or write the system off.

outcomes.headline: This is high-risk. The full obligation set applies.
outcomes.detail: High-risk systems carry the heaviest obligations in the Act: a continuous risk management process, training-data governance, technical documentation, automatic logging, effective human oversight, declared accuracy and robustness, conformity assessment, and post-market monitoring.
actions: Register it in your AI inventory with this rationale and today's date.
Complete an AI risk assessment before it goes further.
Confirm whether you are the provider or the deployer — the obligations differ sharply. {{decision:operator-role}}
Check the timeline — Annex III obligations apply from 2 December 2027, Annex I from 2 August 2028. Work backwards from there.
If personal data is involved, a DPIA is almost certainly required too.

outcomes.headline: High-risk area, but the Article 6(3) narrowing may apply.
outcomes.detail: You are in an Annex III area, which is the default trigger for high-risk status, but you have indicated the system only performs a narrow or preparatory role. That derogation is real — and it is also the most commonly over-claimed provision in the Act.
actions: Treat it as high-risk until you can evidence otherwise. The burden is on you.
Document the assessment of why the derogation applies, and register it — the Act requires this even when you rely on the exemption.
Measure whether humans actually override the output. If the override rate is near zero, the system is not preparatory in practice and the derogation does not hold.
Re-check this decision whenever the system's role expands.
outcomes.counsel: Relying on Article 6(3) is a legal position, not an engineering one. Have it reviewed before you build your compliance programme on it.

outcomes.headline: Limited risk — transparency obligations apply.
outcomes.detail: The system does not carry the high-risk obligation set, but people must be told they are dealing with AI, and AI-generated content must be marked in a machine-readable way.
actions: Add a clear disclosure at the point of interaction, not buried in terms of service.
Mark generated or materially altered content.
Register it in your inventory with this rationale.
Note the date: Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026, with a grace period to 2 December 2026 for systems already in service.

outcomes.headline: Minimal risk. Baseline governance is enough.
outcomes.detail: No specific AI Act obligations attach beyond AI literacy for the people operating it. That is not the same as no governance — it still belongs in your inventory, and your ordinary data protection and security duties are unaffected.
actions: Register it anyway. An unlisted system is one you cannot govern, and classification can change when purpose changes.
Apply your acceptable use policy and data classification rules.
Re-classify if its purpose changes materially.

decisions.title: Are we the provider or the deployer of this system?
decisions.short: Work out which operator role you hold — provider, deployer, importer, or distributor — and record why. The obligations differ sharply.
decisions.why: Almost every obligation in the Act attaches to a role, not to a system. Get this wrong and you either carry duties you do not owe, or miss the ones you do. The common error is assuming that buying a tool always makes you a deployer — fine-tuning it, putting your name on it, or using it for something it was not built for can make you its provider instead.
decisions.intro: Answer about ONE system at a time, and about how you actually use it today. You can hold different roles for different systems, and your role can change if you modify a system later.

questions.text: Did your organisation develop this system, or have it developed for you to your specification?
questions.help: Counts as Yes if you built it in-house, or commissioned it to your own requirements. Counts as No if you bought or subscribed to something that already existed — even if it was configured for you during onboarding.

questions.text: Do you put it on the market or into service under your own name or trade mark?
questions.help: This is the white-labelling trap. If your customers see your brand on a tool that someone else built, you are its provider as far as they and the regulator are concerned — the underlying vendor's role does not shield you.

questions.text: Have you fine-tuned, retrained, or substantially modified the system?
questions.help: Fine-tuning on your own data, retraining, or materially changing how it works all count. Ordinary configuration does not — setting thresholds, choosing which fields it reads, or turning features on and off is normal deployer behaviour.

questions.text: Do you use it for a purpose the vendor did not intend, or in a way that makes it high-risk when it was not sold as such?
questions.help: The example that catches people: a general-purpose text summariser used to rank job applicants. The vendor never intended it for recruitment; by pointing it at that decision, you have changed its intended purpose.

questions.text: Are you established in the EU, or using the system's output inside the EU?
questions.help: Answer Yes if your organisation is in the EU, or if people in the EU are affected by what the system produces. Being outside the EU is not by itself an exemption — the Act reaches output used in the EU.

questions.text: Do you use the system under your own authority — that is, you decide it runs, on whose data, and for what?
questions.help: Answer Yes if you chose to deploy it and control how it is used. Answer No if you merely pass it on to someone else, or use it purely personally and non-professionally.

questions.text: Which of these best describes what you do with it?
questions.help: Pick the closest. These are the value-chain roles for organisations that move a system along rather than operate it.

options.label: We bring it into the EU from a provider based outside the EU
We make it available in the EU, but we did not build or import it
We built it, or had it built to our specification
We only use it ourselves, personally and not for work
None of these — we do operate it ourselves

questions.text: Do you place this system on the EU market, or make it available to anyone in the EU?
questions.help: Includes selling, licensing, or offering it free to EU users. If the answer is genuinely no on every count, the Act does not reach this system — but check with counsel before relying on that.

outcomes.headline: You are the provider of this system.
outcomes.detail: Providers carry the heaviest obligations in the Act. If the system is also high-risk, that means a risk management system, data governance, technical documentation, logging, human oversight design, declared accuracy and robustness, a quality management system, conformity assessment, CE marking, registration, and post-market monitoring.
actions: Record this role against the system in your AI inventory, with today's date.
Classify its risk tier if you have not already — the obligations depend on both.
If it is high-risk, identify your conformity assessment route now. Annex III obligations apply from 2 December 2027 and Annex I from 2 August 2028, and notified-body capacity is finite.
Put a quality management system in place — Art. 17 expects one for high-risk systems.

outcomes.headline: You are the provider, because your name is on it.
outcomes.detail: Putting a system on the market under your own name or trade mark makes you its provider, even though somebody else built it. The original developer's compliance work does not automatically transfer to you.
actions: Record this role and the reason — rebranding — against the system.
Get the underlying provider's technical documentation in writing. You need it to meet obligations that are now yours, and you have a contractual right to ask.
Check your contract flows down the evidence and notification rights you now depend on.
Treat this as a provider obligation set, not a vendor-management exercise.
outcomes.counsel: Where a vendor built the system and you rebrand it, the split of responsibility between you is a contractual question with statutory limits. Have the arrangement reviewed rather than assuming the vendor remains on the hook.

outcomes.headline: You have become the provider by modifying it.
outcomes.detail: Fine-tuning, retraining, or substantially modifying a high-risk system makes you its provider for the modified version. This is the most commonly missed route into provider obligations, because the work feels like ordinary development rather than a change of legal role.
actions: Record this role and what you modified, with the date.
Document the modification — what changed, on what data, and how you evaluated it.
Produce your own technical documentation for the modified system. The original vendor's does not cover your changes.
Re-check the risk tier — modification can change it.
outcomes.counsel: "Substantial modification" is a legal threshold, not an engineering one, and fine-tuning sits close to the line. Confirm where your changes fall before you decide which obligations apply.

outcomes.headline: You are the provider, because you changed what it is for.
outcomes.detail: Using a system for a purpose its vendor did not intend — particularly one that makes it high-risk — makes you the provider of that use. The vendor's documentation covers their intended purpose, not yours.
actions: Record this role and the purpose you are actually using it for.
Re-classify the risk tier against your purpose, not the vendor's description.
Consider whether the intended purpose can be brought back in scope instead. Using the tool as sold is often far cheaper than assuming provider obligations for it.
Produce documentation covering your use, since the vendor's will not.
outcomes.counsel: Whether your use is a genuine change of intended purpose or simply an unusual application is exactly the kind of question worth putting to counsel before you build a compliance programme on the answer.

outcomes.headline: You are the deployer of this system.
outcomes.detail: Deployers use a system under their own authority. The obligations are lighter than a provider's but real: use it per the instructions, assign competent human oversight, keep logs where you control them, monitor operation, and inform the people affected.
actions: Record this role against the system in your AI inventory, with today's date.
Obtain and actually read the provider's instructions for use — your obligations are framed by them.
Assign named human oversight with the competence and authority to override.
If the system is high-risk and you are a public body or provide essential services, check whether you owe a fundamental rights impact assessment under Art. 27.
Tell affected people where transparency duties apply.

outcomes.headline: You are the importer of this system.
outcomes.detail: You bring a system from a non-EU provider into the EU market. Your job is to verify before placing it: that the provider did the conformity assessment, that the documentation and CE marking exist, and that an authorised representative is appointed.
actions: Record this role against the system.
Verify the provider's conformity assessment and technical documentation before placing it on the market.
Keep a copy of the documentation and the certificate for the retention period.
Do not place it if you have reason to believe it is non-conforming — and tell the provider and the authorities if you find out later.

outcomes.headline: You are a distributor of this system.
outcomes.detail: You make a system available on the EU market without being its provider or importer. Your duties are verification-based: check the marking and documentation are present, and act if you learn of a problem.
actions: Record this role against the system.
Verify CE marking and that the provider and importer have met their obligations.
Do not distribute a system you believe to be non-conforming.
Cooperate with authorities and pass on any incident information you receive.

outcomes.headline: This use looks outside the Act's scope — but verify it.
outcomes.detail: On your answers, you neither place this system on the EU market nor use its output in the EU, or your use is purely personal and non-professional. The Act's operator obligations would not attach.
actions: Record the reasoning anyway — scope decisions are exactly what a regulator asks you to evidence.
Re-check if your use, your markets, or the system's purpose change.
Remember other law still applies. Data protection duties are unaffected by AI Act scope.
outcomes.counsel: Territorial scope is the question organisations most often get wrong, because output used in the EU is enough to bring you in. Confirm this one with counsel before relying on it.

eu-ai-act-timeline.title: EU AI Act timeline (2026 Digital Omnibus)

defaults.label: How often governance reports to the board
defaults.value: Quarterly
defaults.unless: Move to monthly while any high-risk system is unassessed, or after a serious incident, until the position is stable again.
defaults.why: Quarterly matches most board cycles, so governance rides an existing meeting rather than competing for a new one. More often than that and you report noise; less often and a problem can run for half a year unseen.

defaults.label: How often the governance committee meets
defaults.value: Monthly
defaults.unless: Quarterly is enough below roughly 150 staff with no high-risk systems. Fortnightly during an active remediation programme.
defaults.why: Monthly keeps decisions moving without the committee becoming the bottleneck. The failure mode is a quarterly committee that becomes the reason nothing ships for eleven weeks.

defaults.label: Quorum for a valid committee decision
defaults.value: Four voting members, and must include the chair (or a named delegate) and Legal/DPO
defaults.unless: In organisations under about 150 staff, three including the chair. Never drop the requirement for a legal or data-protection voice on decisions about personal data.
defaults.why: Without a quorum rule, a committee eventually takes a significant decision with two people in the room, and that decision is the one a regulator asks about.

defaults.label: How far ahead committee papers circulate
defaults.value: Five working days
defaults.unless: Three days for a committee meeting fortnightly or more often.
defaults.why: Late papers are how a committee gets ambushed into approving something nobody read. Deferring late papers by default is the enforcement mechanism.

defaults.label: How often a policy or framework is reviewed
defaults.value: Annually, and on any material change to your AI estate or the law
defaults.unless: Every six months for the Acceptable AI Use Policy while the tool landscape is moving as fast as it currently is.
defaults.why: Annual review is the cadence auditors expect and most organisations can actually sustain. Tying it to material change as well stops a document going stale between reviews.

defaults.label: How long a policy exception lasts before it must be renewed
defaults.value: 90 days
defaults.unless: 30 days where the exception touches a high-risk system or personal data. Never grant one without an expiry date.
defaults.why: An exception with no expiry is a silent policy change. Ninety days is long enough to fix the underlying problem and short enough that nobody forgets it exists.

defaults.label: How often access to data is re-reviewed
defaults.value: Annually for all data; every six months for Restricted
defaults.unless: Quarterly for Restricted data in a regulated sector, or where staff turnover is high.
defaults.why: Access accumulates. Most over-permissioning comes from people changing role rather than from bad initial grants, so the review matters more than the approval.

defaults.label: How fast each incident severity must be picked up
defaults.value: S1 immediately, S2 within 4 hours, S3 within one working day, S4 next cycle
defaults.unless: Tighten S1 and S2 if you operate a 24/7 service or your sector sets shorter supervisory reporting windows.
defaults.why: The Art. 73 serious-incident clock starts when you establish the link between system and incident, not when you finish investigating. Slow triage burns the reporting window before anyone realises it is running.

defaults.label: When to decide whether an incident is reportable
defaults.value: Within 24 hours of detection, in parallel with fixing it
defaults.unless: Immediately if the incident involves harm to a person or special category data.
defaults.why: Reportability is a separate decision from remediation and must not queue behind it. Assessing early and recording the reasoning protects you even if the answer is "not reportable".

defaults.label: How long AI system logs are retained
defaults.value: Six months minimum; twelve months for high-risk systems
defaults.unless: Longer where your sector's record-keeping rules or your limitation period require it. Shorter is rarely defensible for a high-risk system.
defaults.why: Art. 12 expects logs sufficient to trace behaviour over the system's lifetime. A challenge to a decision usually arrives months after it was made, so shorter retention means you cannot answer it.

defaults.label: How often a high-risk system is re-assessed
defaults.value: Annually, and on any material change of purpose, data, or model
defaults.unless: Every six months where the model is retrained frequently or the vendor ships model changes without notice.
defaults.why: Risk assessment under Art. 9 is a continuous process, not a launch gate. Tying review to material change catches the drift an annual date misses.

defaults.label: How often the AI inventory is swept for new systems
defaults.value: Quarterly, including a review of vendor release notes
defaults.unless: Monthly if you have a large SaaS estate or an active procurement pipeline.
defaults.why: Most organisations' fastest-growing AI exposure is features switched on inside software they already licence. Nobody procured them as AI, so only a deliberate sweep finds them.

defaults.label: How quickly a vendor must tell you about an incident
defaults.value: 24 hours for critical vendors; 72 hours otherwise
defaults.unless: Match the tightest window that applies to you — if your own regulator gives you 72 hours, a vendor telling you at 72 hours is already too late.
defaults.why: Your reporting clock may already be running while you wait to hear. This is the clause most worth spending negotiating capital on.

defaults.label: How often vendor AI risk is reassessed
defaults.value: Annually for critical vendors, and at every contract renewal
defaults.unless: Immediately whenever a vendor announces new AI functionality in a product you already use.
defaults.why: Renewal is the only moment you reliably have leverage, so tie the assessment to it rather than to an arbitrary date.

defaults.label: What proportion of relevant staff should complete AI literacy training
defaults.value: 90% of staff who build, buy, or operate AI, within 12 months
defaults.unless: 100% where staff make or materially inform decisions about individuals — there is no acceptable untrained minority in that group.
defaults.why: Art. 4 has been in force since February 2025 and applies regardless of risk tier. Ninety percent is achievable and measurable; chasing the last ten percent of a general population costs more than it returns.

defaults.label: How long approving a new AI tool should take
defaults.value: Five working days
defaults.unless: Ten days where the tool will process personal data and needs a DPIA.
defaults.why: Slow approval produces shadow AI, which is worse than the risk you were managing. Publishing the turnaround is what makes people willing to ask.

defaults.label: What data quality threshold to set
defaults.value: 98% completeness and 99% validity on data feeding a high-risk AI system
defaults.unless: Set thresholds from use, not ambition. Data feeding an internal dashboard can sit far lower; data feeding a regulatory return should be higher.
defaults.why: A threshold nobody measures is worse than none, because it implies assurance you do not have. Start with two dimensions on your two most important domains.

defaults.label: How often controls are tested
defaults.value: Annually for high-risk controls; a risk-based sample for the rest
defaults.unless: Quarterly for any control that has failed in the last twelve months.
defaults.why: Testing design once and operation annually is the minimum that supports a genuine assurance opinion. Re-testing what has already failed is where the value is.

defaults.label: How long to keep personal data by default
defaults.value: Only as long as the stated purpose requires, with a documented period per activity
defaults.unless: Your sector sets a statutory minimum — those override any shorter period you would otherwise choose.
defaults.why: "As long as necessary" is not a retention period. A named number per activity is what makes deletion enforceable and defensible.

defaults.label: How long two functions get to resolve a disagreement before it escalates
defaults.value: Five working days, then the governance lead facilitates for a further five
defaults.unless: Escalate immediately where a live system is causing harm — do not run the clock during an incident.
defaults.why: Unresolved disagreement is the most common reason a control quietly stops operating. A timebox forces it upward instead of letting it stall.

defaults.label: How quickly a system suspension must be reported to the committee
defaults.value: Within 24 hours of the suspension, never before it
defaults.unless: Nothing. Notification always follows the stop.
defaults.why: If stopping a system requires permission first, it will not happen in time. Distributing the right to suspend and requiring prompt notification afterwards is what makes the control real.

defaults.label: How soon after a serious incident to hold the review
defaults.value: Within 10 working days for S1 and S2
defaults.unless: Within 5 working days if the incident is still open or a regulator has been notified — the facts fade fast and you may need them.
defaults.why: Long enough for the immediate fix to be done and the facts to settle, short enough that people still remember what happened. Beyond about a fortnight the review turns into a documentation exercise.

defaults.label: How many affected people should trigger board-level escalation
defaults.value: 10,000 people, or any amount of special category data
defaults.unless: Lower it to match your own breach-notification threshold if you already have one — running two different numbers guarantees the wrong one gets used.
defaults.why: A round number people remember beats a precise one they look up. The special-category carve-out matters more than the count: a handful of health records can be graver than ten thousand email addresses.

defaults.label: How quickly an urgent decision must be ratified by the committee
defaults.value: Within 48 hours
defaults.unless: Next working day if the decision suspended a live customer-facing system.
defaults.why: Someone has already acted without permission — correctly, because the alternative was waiting during an incident. Ratifying quickly is what keeps that emergency power legitimate rather than habitual.

defaults.label: At what residual risk rating the committee, rather than an owner, must accept it
defaults.value: A residual rating of 10 or above on a 5x5 scale (High and Critical)
defaults.unless: Align to your enterprise risk framework's own escalation point if you have one, so the same risk does not get two different treatments.
defaults.why: Below High, an accountable owner accepting risk is proportionate and fast. At High and above the consequence is organisational, so the acceptance should be too — and it should be minuted with a name against it.

defaults.label: How long governance should take to reach a decision on a new system
defaults.value: A median of 10 working days from intake to decision
defaults.unless: 20 days for high-risk systems, which genuinely need a fuller assessment — but publish the longer target rather than quietly missing the shorter one.
defaults.why: This is the metric that decides whether people route around you. Slow governance produces shadow AI, which is a worse risk than the one you were managing.

defaults.label: What proportion of systems should pass a governance gate first time
defaults.unless: Expect lower in the first two quarters while teams learn what is expected. Persistently below 50% means your standards are unclear, not that your teams are careless.
defaults.why: A very high pass rate suggests the gate is not testing anything. A very low one suggests the requirements were never communicated. Around 70% is the band where the gate is doing real work.

defaults.label: What human override rate indicates oversight is genuinely working
defaults.value: Between 2% and 20%
defaults.unless: Judge it per system rather than globally. What matters is that the rate is monitored and explicable, not that it sits in any particular band.
defaults.why: Below 2% the reviewer is almost certainly approving by default, which is the most common way Art. 14 human oversight fails in practice. Above 20% the model is not fit for the decision it is being used for.

defaults.label: How many high or critical risks should be open past their target date
defaults.value: Zero
defaults.unless: Nothing. A risk past its own remediation date is either being treated or should be formally re-accepted with a new date and a named acceptor.
defaults.why: This is one of the few metrics where the target is genuinely zero. A non-zero number is not a performance issue — it means a decision has quietly expired.

defaults.label: How many governance reports the board should receive each year
defaults.value: Four
defaults.unless: Add an extraordinary report after any S1 incident or regulatory contact, rather than waiting for the next scheduled one.
defaults.why: Matches the quarterly reporting cadence and most board calendars. Fewer than four and a problem can run most of a year unseen by the people accountable for it.
